articles.title: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row
articles.summary: The much-loved shopkeeper has been seen but not heard around Springfield for eight years, until now.
articles.body:
The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.

The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.

Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.

The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.

Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.

The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient.

Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.

Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."

Speaking to Variety ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink.

"But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"

The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?

"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"

After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026.

"It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."

Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar - who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show - taking over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.

In Apu's haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on French electro duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents.

A year on he returns to wreak his revenge.

Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes off his helmet and reveals himself to be Apu.

He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick.

"I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.

articles.title: In 2018, Indian-origin siblings Rohan and Anya Satija sold cookies and lemonade in Texas to buy books; their nonprofit has now donated 100,000 books and 125,000 supplies and classroom items, helping 15,000 students
articles.summary: An Austin lemonade stand started by two young siblings in 2018 has grown into an educational non-profit that has shared 100,000 books, 125,000 learning
articles.body: An Austin lemonade stand started by two young siblings in 2018 has grown into an educational non-profit that has shared 100,000 books, 125,000 learning supplies, and thousands of mental health kits across Texas. Indian-origin brother and sister Rohan and Anya Satija began their work after learning about "book deserts." These are neighbourhoods where children have limited access to books suited to their age. What started as a small local fundraising effort soon grew into the Let's Learn Foundation, a non-profit that now works with 13 Texas school districts, hospitals, and youth centres. According to figures published by Global Indian, the foundation has directly reached more than 15,000 students. It provides books, classroom supplies, and kits to support emotional well-being in low-income and underserved communities.Personal struggles inspiring community actionThe idea for the non-profit came from Rohan Satija's own experience of adjusting to life in the United States. After his family moved from New Zealand to Austin, Texas, in 2018, Rohan struggled with anxiety and panic attacks because of the sudden change in culture and surroundings. Books gave him comfort during this difficult time and helped him understand his unfamiliar surroundings. During a middle school project, he learned that many children in his local community did not have enough reading materials. This inspired him to take action. “I was alarmed to hear of the prevalence of book deserts in Texas,” Rohan told Global Indian. “I found comfort in books and storytelling, but I was alarmed to hear of the prevalence of book deserts in Texas, areas where reading materials are difficult to obtain.” Rohan, who was then 10 years old, joined forces with his sister Anya, who was two years younger. At first, they baked cookies and sold lemonade in their neighbourhood to raise money to buy books. Within nine months, their small community effort had grown into a registered non-profit organisation working to reduce educational inequality.Expansion into mental health and youth advocacyOver the past six years, the siblings have expanded the foundation's work beyond reading and literacy. They have added mental health support to their programmes and started providing resources to help students manage their emotions. Understanding that school performance and emotional well-being are closely connected, the team began preparing and distributing special mental health kits to schools. “Mental health and education are deeply intertwined,” Rohan explained to Global Indian. “By addressing both simultaneously, we can create environments where students are not just learning but thriving.” The foundation has also started the Vibrant Voices Project, a creative writing and theatre programme at the Hays County Juvenile Centre. It encourages young people in detention to work through mental health challenges by writing and performing monologues based on their own experiences. “This program emphasizes the impact that storytelling can have on youth mental health, fostering therapeutic self-expression and reducing mental health stigma,” Rohan said.Institutional partnerships and corporate supportThe Let's Learn Foundation has grown with help from partnerships with educational publishers and national charitable organisations. It has worked with Scholastic to obtain large quantities of reading materials. It has also received financial support and grants from Lady Gaga's Born This Way Foundation. The non-profit also works with local medical and social support organisations, including Dell Children's Hospital, Active Minds, and SAFE Austin. These partnerships help ensure that books and care packages reach children facing difficult situations. Alongside his work with the foundation, Rohan has taken on public advisory roles focused on youth mental health policies. He is the youngest representative on the Texas Children and Youth Behavioural Health Subcommittee and is also a member of the Williamson County Child and Youth Behavioural Health Taskforce. He has also led workshops at regional mental health conferences, including the 2023 NAMI Texas Conference.Future goals and ongoing campaignsDespite gaining national attention and corporate support, the Satija siblings continue to organise local donation drives and manage the delivery of supplies to schools themselves. “The real reward is seeing the joy on children's face when they receive their first book or realizing that our mental health kits are helping students feel supported,” Rohan told Global Indian. According to figures published on the Let's Learn Foundation's official website, the organisation plans to expand its distribution network to more school districts across central Texas. It will focus on rural communities and low-income urban areas where access to public libraries remains limited. As the siblings balance their high school studies with running the non-profit, their main goal remains the same. “We want to ensure that every child, no matter their background, has the resources they need to learn, grow, and succeed,” Rohan said.You use AI every day. articles.summary: BHUBANESWAR: Leader of opposition and BJD president Naveen Patnaik on Monday wrote to chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi, questioning the state
articles.body: BHUBANESWAR: Leader of opposition and BJD president Naveen Patnaik on Monday wrote to chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi, questioning the state government’s silence after Andhra Pradesh announced panchayat elections that could extend to disputed villages in Kotia, “an integral part of Odisha”.In the letter dated Oct 19, Patnaik asked what had become of the BJP’s pre-2024 manifesto promise that a “double engine government” would resolve the Kotia issue “once and for all” and restore "Odia Swabhiman". He asked whether the “Go Back Andhra” slogan was merely a gimmick to win votes.Is political dependence the reason?Patnaik pointed out that the Telugu Desam Party, which governs Andhra Pradesh, is a crucial ally of the BJP-led NDA government at the Centre, whose majority it helps sustain. He asked whether this dependence explained the Odisha government’s silence and its willingness to compromise the state’s interests. He also sought the recommendations of the 16-member Kotia Committee constituted in 2025 and the action taken on them.What is the Kotia dispute?Kotia panchayat, under Pottangi block of Koraput district, has 28 villages. Odisha maintains that all of them belong to Koraput, while Andhra Pradesh claims 21 and extends administrative services to residents, identifying several settlements by different names. The dispute has lasted for decades.Why is it back in focus?The Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission has announced rural polls in three phases on Nov 26, 29 and Dec 2, covering Parvathipuram Manyam district, which includes villages claimed by both states. However, polling dates for the disputed Kotia villages have not been specified. Pottangi tehsildar DBS Dharua said the administration was monitoring developments and “necessary action will be taken”.Legal backdropThe dispute reached the Supreme Court in 1968, which directed both states to maintain status quo. Tensions escalated in Feb 2021 when Andhra held panchayat elections in the disputed villages, prompting Odisha to approach the apex court, alleging violation of the status quo.Pressure mounts on BJPCongress has also targeted the government. Koraput MP Saptagiri Sankar Ulaka asked why Odisha was silent when the BJP was in power in Odisha and at the Centre and was part of the ruling alliance in Andhra. Pottangi MLA Ram Chandra Kadam urged resolving the issue through dialogue, while Jeypore MLA Tara Prasad Bahinipati warned of a mass agitation if the government failed to act.BJP functionary Goutam Samantaray said the government was committed to protecting Odisha’s territorial integrity and was monitoring developments. articles.title: A rare 1937 first edition of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit was found during a Bristol house clearance; the book sold for £43,000 at auction
articles.summary: A rare first-edition copy of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit was discovered during a house clearance in Bristol and sold for £43,000 at auction in August 2025.
articles.body: A rare first-edition copy of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit was discovered during a house clearance in Bristol and sold for £43,000 at auction in August 2025. The book, one of 1,500 copies printed in September 1937, had been overlooked among other titles in a private collection. Auctioneum, the auction house that identified the volume, had estimated it would sell for between £10,000 and £12,000. Competitive bidding pushed the hammer price to about 3.6 times the upper estimate and 4.3 times the lower one. The copy had no dust jacket, making the result notable in the rare-book market. Auctioneum linked the book’s provenance to botanist Hubert Priestley and suggested a possible connection between the Priestley family and Tolkien through Oxford circles. The precise nature of that connection remains unclear.How a rare Hobbit first edition was discovered during a Bristol house clearanceThe discovery came during a routine house clearance after the property’s owner had died. According to the specialist antiques publication Antiques Trade Gazette, Auctioneum managing director Evan McPherson was at the address when he sent photographs of a possible find to book specialist Caitlin Riley. The book had been lying in an old Globe-Wernicke lawyer’s cabinet among reference books, cooking books and children’s titles. The volume was identified as a first impression of the 1937 edition. A first impression refers to copies produced in the initial printing, distinguishing them from later printings of the same edition.Riley described the book as being in “absolutely beautiful condition”, although reports noted that its spine was slightly discoloured. She also described it as being in “absolutely beautiful condition”, although the book’s spine was reported to be slightly discoloured. The volume’s provenance added interest to the discovery. It came from the family library of Hubert Priestley, a botanist. Auctioneum suggested that Priestley and Tolkien may have known each other through Oxford connections and that both had correspondence involving C.S. Lewis. That account should be treated as the auction house’s proposed connection, rather than proof that Priestley and Tolkien personally knew one another. Further archival evidence would be needed to establish the nature of their relationship.Why a first edition of The Hobbit is so rareThe Hobbit was first published in September 1937. Auctioneum says the initial print run comprised 1,500 copies and that only a few hundred are believed to survive. The small original print run and the scarcity of surviving copies help explain why authentic first impressions attract collectors. The Bristol copy was bound in light green cloth and featured black-and-white illustrations. Its status as a first impression distinguishes it from later printings of the same edition. Distinguishing an original first impression from a later edition or facsimile is essential when establishing a rare book’s value. The absence of a dust jacket did not prevent the copy from attracting strong bidding. Dust jackets can be important to collectors because they are vulnerable to damage and loss, and copies retaining their original jackets can command higher prices. The Bristol sale was reported as a record for an unsigned first edition without its dust jacket, rather than a record for all first editions of the novel.The book introduced readers to Bilbo Baggins and the fictional world Tolkien developed further in The Lord of the Rings. Its continuing popularity has helped sustain demand for early editions, particularly those with distinctive provenance or inscriptions. A separate first edition of The Hobbit, containing a handwritten note in Elvish by Tolkien, sold at Sotheby’s in 2015 for £137,000. Its inscription distinguished it from the Bristol copy, making the two results difficult to compare directly. A signed first edition sold for $300,000 at Heritage Auctions in 2024, providing a more recent high-value comparison, although differences in condition, provenance and inscriptions should be considered.The Hobbit auction result: £43,000 against a £10,000 to £12,000 estimateThe Bristol copy was sold in a timed online auction run by Auctioneum in Bath, which ended on August 6, 2025. Its estimate was £10,000 to £12,000. The £43,000 hammer price was £31,000 above the upper estimate, or about 3.6 times that estimate. Compared with the lower estimate, it was approximately 4.3 times as much. The buyer was a private collector based in the United Kingdom. Auctioneum reported international interest in the book, with competition among bidders helping to drive the price above expectations.The hammer price was not the same as the buyer’s total bill. Antiques Trade Gazette reported a total of £52,030 with fees, £9,030 more than the winning bid. The distinction is important when comparing auction results, because fees and premiums can make the amount paid by the buyer higher than the price announced when the lot sells. The discovery offers a practical lesson for anyone sorting through an inherited library or an old collection. Books should not be judged solely by their appearance or by the shelf on which they are found. Publication dates, printing details, publisher information, illustrations, inscriptions and provenance can all affect their value.Anyone who suspects that a book may be a valuable early edition should preserve it and seek an assessment from a rare-book specialist or established auction house before selling or discarding it. The Bristol copy’s journey from an overlooked household item to a £43,000 auction result shows how careful identification can reveal the significance of a seemingly ordinary book.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
articles.summary: The independent politician is in hospital after what the prime minister says may have been a deliberate attack.
articles.body:
Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack.

The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.

Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".

Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".

While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia.

His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.

Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.

The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.

A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars .

Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.

After being subdued and detained by the passerby, the suspect was arrested by police.

Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act.

"It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."

Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car

Although not necessarily a household name across Australia, in the political sphere Helen Haines is both well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner.

There has been an outpouring of messages from politicians and party leaders across the breadth of the political spectrum. In an age of increasingly divisive politics, she is seen by many as a unifying force.

The independent MP has only been a federal parliamentarian for a relatively short time, having been elected in 2019. However, in that time she has become an influential advocate for integrity in politics.

Haines proposed legislation for a national anti-corruption watchdog in 2021, and has been credited for driving the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission under Labor in the previous parliamentary term.

She currently sits on the parliamentary committee responsible for its oversight.

Haines has often banded together with other key independents on issues that include climate action and gender equality.

Allegra Spender, another independent MP who has collaborated with Haines, called her "the best of us".

An Australian parliamentary report warned last year that threats and physical attacks had increased "significantly over the past decade".

A threat assessment by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation - the country's equivalent of MI5 in the UK - warned last year that the risk of politically motivated violence was "already flashing red".

Albanese became emotional as he talked about Haines in a live television interview on ABC's 7:30.

He appeared close to tears when asked whether he and his colleagues talked among themselves about the threats and risks they face.

"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one, one of my colleagues."

He described Haines as having "integrity". In other political reaction:

Opposition leader Angus Taylor - head of the Liberal Party - said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the news, and that Australians would be "angry and appalled by the attack on Helen"

Senator Matt Canavan, leader of The Nationals, said his heart went out to Haines and her family "upon the news of this shocking attack"

Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge said he was "horrified" to hear of the "apparent attack", adding: "Helen is an extraordinary human being and brings people together like few others"

Senator Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader, said violence against elected representatives is "never acceptable". She added: "Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety"

articles.title: France PM calls for partial curfews after violent weekend protests
articles.summary: The country's interior minister admits that police "lost control" in some cities amid riots and looting.
articles.body:
France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews to protect people and shops after a weekend of riots and looting across the country.

Marseille - the country's second-largest city - has already banned public gatherings between 12:00 and 20:00.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, whose resignation offer was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, earlier admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. More than 2,500 people were arrested, officials said. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

The disorder began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but protests have since escalated to take in a broader range of concerns.

Protesters were also hurt during clashes with police, with one demonstrator's hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency.

Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews "where they need", without specifying which cities would be impacted.

Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage, and the funding would be recovered from those behind the violence.

"There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay," the prime minister said.

He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work as a result of the riots and looting.

Meanwhile, Nuñez said some 200 investigators were analysing CCTV footage to try to identify possible ringleaders of the violent protests.

Nuñez attempted to resign on Sunday, but Macron refused "given the need for continued command of law enforcement", the Élysée Palace said.

More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) says.

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that damage from the riots was estimated at "hundreds of millions of euros".

Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets over the weekend for protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.

Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris on Sunday, according to the AFP, and bottles and rocks were hurled at police.

In the central city of Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing as the flames took hold.

"It's awful and unbelievable," said a local resident who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."

President Macron said on Sunday that a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of peaceful protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".

articles.title: Southport killer faces trial for alleged prison attacks
articles.summary: Axel Rudakubana appeared at Monday's hearing via a videolink from Broadmoor Hospital.
articles.body:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana is due to face trial next year over allegations he threw boiling water mixed with sugar at a prison officer.

Rudakubana, who is serving a life sentence for the murders of three young girls in 2024, appeared via videolink at the Old Bailey on Monday where he spoke only to confirm his name.

He has been charged with attempted grievous bodily harm of a prison officer, two other assaults of officers and possession of a knife or other offensive weapon across separate dates last year at HMP Belmarsh, south London.

Rudakubana was not asked to enter any pleas and a preliminary hearing has been set for 5 February, with a provisional trial date of 8 October 2027.

Rudakubana, 20, is serving a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

On 8 May last year, it is alleged he threw hot water through a hatch in his prison cell door.

It is further alleged that two days before, on 6 May, Rudakubana threatened to "soak" a female officer outside his cell if she did not pass him a newspaper and then threw liquid at her.

Rudakubana also allegedly punched a male officer on 28 October.

The offensive weapon charge relates to sharpened stone shards that the prosecution say had seemingly been prised from the floor of the defendant's cell.

In July, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh, where the attacks allegedly took place, to Broadmoor high-security psychiatric hospital.

articles.title: A 23-year-old spent $120 turning a free Facebook Marketplace find into a pill bottle table; the design generated $150,000 in sales in two weeks
articles.summary: A piece of furniture does not usually begin with a free object found on Facebook Marketplace, a little foam and a sheet of printed paper.
articles.body: A piece of furniture does not usually begin with a free object found on Facebook Marketplace, a little foam and a sheet of printed paper. For Oskar Flodstrom, a 23-year-old artist based in Los Angeles, those inexpensive materials became the starting point for an unusual pill bottle-shaped side table. He had been making music and experimenting with art while working as a swimming instructor to cover his expenses. Furniture was not a business he had set out to build. Yet a video showing his creation eventually attracted enormous attention online, bringing sales that he had not anticipated. In a conversation with Entrepreneur, the product generated $150,000 in gross sales over two weeks, following an initial investment of roughly $120.How Flodstrom developed his creative interests outside collegeFlodstrom had enjoyed drawing and making things since childhood, though he did not initially see art as a practical career. Engineering briefly appeared to offer a compromise between creativity and a more conventional profession. The disruption caused by the pandemic during his final year of high school also influenced his next steps. He decided not to attend college, citing the expense and doubts about whether a degree would help him pursue his interests. Instead, he began making music, drawing inspiration from American record producer and DJ Kenny Beats, while working out how to support himself.Teaching swimming lessons provided a source of income. His creative projects continued alongside the job, but they did not immediately develop into a reliable business. Flodstrom was still experimenting with different materials and ideas, without a clear route from making art to earning money from it.A free find from Facebook Marketplace became furnitureThe idea for the pill bottle table emerged while Flodstrom was looking for inexpensive ways to furnish his apartment. Browsing Facebook Marketplace, he came across a clear, rounded acrylic base being offered for free. He did not have a car, so collecting it meant travelling by bus and carrying the object home himself.Flodstrom had an idea of the shape he wanted but had not settled on the materials needed to complete it. Eventually, he used foam for the upper section and added paint and a paper label to make the piece resemble an oversized medicine bottle.The finished object was assembled on a modest budget. Since the acrylic base cost nothing, the remaining materials accounted for most of the approximately $120 he spent bringing the design together. The printed label alone cost around $12, according to his account to Entrepreneur.It was an unconventional piece of furniture, but the concept was straightforward. A familiar household object had been enlarged and repurposed as a table. The design also left room for other uses, something that would become important when Flodstrom began showing it to a wider audience.How Flodstrom turned discarded materials into creative furnitureThe pill bottle table was not Flodstrom's first attempt at making furniture from discarded or inexpensive materials. He had previously created a chair resembling an avocado, which sold for around $500. He had also found useful objects left on the street in Los Angeles, where people sometimes leave unwanted belongings outside when moving home.These projects were part of his wider interest in making things rather than an established furniture business. At first, he considered placing the pill bottle table in the background of a music video. He eventually decided to document its construction instead, using the process as material for a social media post under his creative name, Erik Oskr.The video gave viewers a way to see how the object came together, rather than presenting it simply as a finished product.A manufacturing partnership helped turn the design into a productThe original video attracted attention in June 2026, bringing Flodstrom's work to the notice of NO LOGO, a company that helps creators and businesses develop products without having to establish their own manufacturing facilities.The company offered to produce a sample using photographs and measurements of his design. During the process, the partners made a change to the lid material to improve its stability. NO LOGO also helped Flodstrom establish a Shopify website through which customers could buy the table.Until then, the project had largely been an individual experiment. Developing a version that could be sold required a different set of decisions, including how to reproduce the design and present it as a commercial product.Flodstrom was still living out of a car he had bought when the sample arrived, having found himself between places to stay. A representative from the company asked whether he would take part in an interview about the table. He agreed, without expecting the conversation to lead to much.Instagram views surged after Flodstrom showed a new use for his tableWhen the table was ready to sell, Flodstrom began preparing more videos to introduce it to potential customers. The early results were disappointing. Instagram flagged one of the promotional videos because the bottle carried an Adderall label, complicating his initial attempt to reach an audience.He had expected to make at least 10 to 15 sales on the first day. Instead, around 36 hours passed with only a couple of orders coming through. The response was considerably smaller than he had anticipated, and the first promotional videos had done little to change that.In his interview with Entrepreneur, Flodstrom recalled Instagram generating around one million views per hour for approximately 10 consecutive hours. He attributed roughly 200 sales to the surge in attention.The sudden change in response was striking compared with the slow opening days. A product that had struggled to attract buyers was now reaching viewers at a pace he had not previously experienced.The pill bottle table generated $150,000 in two weeksAccording to Entrepreneur's September 17, 2026 report, the pill bottle table brought in $150,000 in gross sales over a two-week period. That figure refers to revenue from sales, rather than the amount Flodstrom personally earned after manufacturing expenses and other costs.He told the publication that daily sales had subsequently settled into a range of approximately $1,500 to $4,000, depending partly on advertising activity. NO LOGO takes a portion to cover manufacturing costs, while Flodstrom estimated that his margin was about five times larger than the company's cut. The report did not provide a detailed breakdown of expenses or net profit.The commercial response gave him an opportunity to build on a project that had started with a free acrylic base. It also left him with a new set of questions about what to make next and whether the initial attention could be sustained.Plans for more unconventional household productsFlodstrom has said he does not want to be known exclusively for the pill bottle table. He sees it as an early step in a broader effort to develop products from ideas that might otherwise remain personal art projects.Among the concepts he mentioned to Entrepreneur were a large mirror shaped like a razor blade and a lava lamp made from a Sprite bottle. He had also created a bong from a milk jug. The ideas reflect the same interest in transforming recognisable everyday objects into something with a different purpose or appearance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2020, an Ohio couple moved into a friend's home and spent $30,000 on its kitchen; six years later, an appeals court rejected their $215,000 purchase claim and revived the owners' eviction bid
articles.summary: In 2020, an Ohio couple moved into a friend's home and spent $30,000 on its kitchen; six years later, an appeals court rejected their $215,000 purchase
articles.body: In 2020, an Ohio couple moved into a friend's home and spent $30,000 on its kitchen; six years later, an appeals court rejected their $215,000 purchase claim and revived the owners' eviction bidA couple in Ohio, who moved into a friend's house and spent $30,000 renovating its kitchen, have lost their claim to purchase the property for $215,000. Six years after they first moved in 2020, an appeals court ruled that the money spent on renovations did not give them a legal right to buy the house. The Wednesday decision also allowed the homeowners to pursue their eviction claim.The dispute involved Carl and Lane Claxton and their friends, James and Beverly Lupinetti, where an arrangement to help the Claxtons buy a house eventually turned into a disagreement over money, renovations, and ownership. According to court records, the Claxtons believed they had an agreement to purchase the property, while the Lupinettis maintained that the sale had never been completed.The matter reached court in April 2022, when James Lupinetti sought to evict the Claxtons from his Blue Meadow Lane property. The couple challenged the eviction and insisted that the house was supposed to be sold to them. In September 2025, a lower court ruled in their favour and ordered the homeowners to complete the $215,000 sale.However, the Ohio First District Court of Appeals overturned that decision. It found that the families had never entered into a binding agreement to sell the house. Although the Claxtons could no longer enforce the proposed purchase, the judges said they could still receive compensation for improvements made to the property.Friendship led to housing arrangementJames Lupinetti and Carl Claxton had known each other for nearly a decade before the dispute began. They met while playing basketball at a YMCA around 2010 or 2011 and became friends.In 2019, James faced financial difficulties after his dump truck business failed. Carl, who had invested in the business, lent him $10,000. James agreed to repay $15,000, including interest.By 2020, James and Beverly had moved into a condominium, leaving their house on Blue Meadow Lane vacant. James was concerned about losing the property because he was struggling financially.At the time, mortgage payments on the house had been temporarily suspended under a Covid-19 relief programme. Carl expressed interest in buying the property, and the two families began discussing an arrangement.The Claxtons moved into the house in October 2020. They were allowed to live there without making housing payments until May 2021, when the mortgage relief period ended. James understood that this arrangement would also settle the earlier loan.After May 2021, the Claxtons began making payments directly to the mortgage lender while trying to arrange financing to purchase the house.The $30,000 kitchen renovationWhile living in the property, the Claxtons began making changes to the house. They painted rooms, repaired damaged flooring and walls, worked on the septic system and renovated the kitchen. Both families later agreed in court that the kitchen renovation had cost $30,000.The Claxtons said they made the improvements because they believed the house would eventually belong to them. James, however, testified that he became concerned when he discovered the kitchen work in October 2021 because the couple had not yet purchased the property. He also told the court that he was willing to pay $30,000 for the improvements.Meanwhile, the proposed purchase was running into difficulties. The Claxtons obtained preliminary approval for a $215,000 mortgage, but a vehicle loan affected their ability to secure financing.They subsequently sold their Yukon truck in an attempt to resolve the problem. The families also signed documents in December 2021 outlining the proposed sale, but those documents specifically stated that they were not legally binding.Further attempts to arrange financing followed, including assistance from Carl's friend Ray Wilkins. However, the sale still did not go ahead. The parties gave different accounts of the financing problems and disagreements over the purchase price. On February 22, 2022, James informed Carl that he would no longer sell him the house.How the failed purchase became an eviction disputeThe collapse of the sale left the Claxtons living in a property they had hoped to own. In April 2022, James filed an eviction case, claiming that the couple owed $8,314.55 in unpaid rent.The Claxtons opposed the eviction. They argued that the homeowners had agreed to sell them the property and that the renovations supported their claim.The lower court initially accepted their position. In September 2025, it ordered the Lupinettis to sell the house for $215,000 and rejected the eviction claim. The homeowners appealed, bringing the dispute before the Ohio First District Court of Appeals.Why appeals court rejected purchase claimThe judges found that the families had never signed a binding agreement to sell the house. Although the Claxtons had lived there, paid towards the mortgage and spent money on renovations, these actions were not enough to establish that the homeowners were legally required to sell it to them.The court also noted that the mortgage payments were connected to the couple's stay in the property rather than payments towards the purchase price.As for the renovations, the judges found that spending money on improvements did not automatically establish ownership rights.The court also concluded that the Claxtons were tenants because they had agreed to pay the mortgage and utilities while occupying the house. Their failure to make the agreed payments for several months meant that the homeowners were entitled to pursue eviction.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tucson’s 17-storey luxury tower opened in 1963 before becoming public housing; 63 years later, residents move into renovated apartments as part of its 358-unit overhaul
articles.summary: A landmark 17-storey building in Tucson, Arizona, is entering a new era, with residents beginning to move into renovated units as part of a major project
articles.body: A landmark 17-storey building in Tucson, Arizona, is entering a new era, with residents beginning to move into renovated units as part of a major project to provide affordable housing for older adults.Tucson House, located at 1501 N. Oracle Road, welcomed 25 households into 24 newly renovated apartments on its 15th floor, just 10 months after officials launched a comprehensive rehabilitation project. The renovations will modernise the ageing building, improve accessibility and ensure it continues to provide affordable homes for decades to come. The project will provide 358 affordable apartments for people aged 55 and older and is expected to be completed by summer 2028.The move marks the first major step in renovating Tucson House. The City of Tucson’s Housing and Community Development Department, El Pueblo Housing Development and Gorman & Company are leading the project to preserve affordable homes for older adults for years to come.“This project is not just about preserving housing; it’s about transforming public housing into something sustainable, dignified, and built for the future. We are grateful to the residents who have been patient with construction and who can now live in and enjoy a safe, beautiful home,” Mayor Regina Romero said in a release.From luxury high-rise to public housingBuilt in 1963, the 17-storey tower opened as private luxury apartments. Over the decades, it became public housing managed by the City of Tucson. The tower became home to many older adults and residents with mobility challenges. The building aged along with them.A 2019 physical assessment concluded that conditions had continued to deteriorate. The building needed major reinvestment to remain part of the city’s housing portfolio. In July 2023, federal assistance arrived when the US Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Tucson a $50 million Choice Neighbourhoods Implementation Grant. The funding provided the foundation for the rehabilitation and a wider neighbourhood plan.Ten months after work began, 25 households are moving into the renovated apartments on the 15th floor. This is, of course, a small beginning to a project that will take years. However, it is the first time the work has produced apartments that residents can move into.Three more floors are due to be handed over by the end of 2026: the 13th, 14th and 16th. Overall completion is scheduled for summer 2028, and the city says more than a quarter of the work has already been completed.Inside the new apartmentsThe finished building will contain 358 apartments for residents aged 55 and older. The units range from studios to two-bedroom homes, measuring between 464 and 975 sq ft. Each apartment will have new flooring, countertops, cabinets, appliances, bathrooms, lighting and its own heating and cooling unit. The crew is also replacing the building’s mechanical, plumbing and electrical systems.The shared spaces are also being updated. Planned amenities include a laundry room, a lounge, a mailroom, a fitness room, a landscaped courtyard, an updated pool and multipurpose rooms for resident services. The original architectural elements of the 1963 building will be preserved in the entrance lobby. The 17th-floor gathering space will have a kitchenette, a television and panoramic views of the city. Some common areas are expected to open in late 2026 and early 2027.Tucson House residents are thrilled about their fresh start in a modernised home.“I’ve lived here for four and a half years, and the building really needed this remodel,” said Donald Burrow, 62, who currently works with the construction team. “The old units are still good homes, but they needed the work. The apartments upstairs are beautiful, and Gorman is doing a really good job on the renovation. I just bought a couch, and I’m so excited to move from my studio into a one-bedroom apartment. I go upstairs every day to check out the renovations, and I can’t wait to move in.”HCD Director Ann Chanecka also reflected on the progress. “Rehabilitating Tucson House has been a complex undertaking, with significant challenges along the way. Seeing 25 households move into their newly renovated apartments is an important milestone and a testament to the collaboration between HCD and our partners. This work is about more than improving a building; it’s about ensuring Tucson House residents have a safe, dignified place to call home.”“Gorman & Company is thrilled to celebrate the rehabilitation of the 15th floor, the first of 17 floors within the historic Tucson House revitalisation project,” said Sally Schwenn, Arizona Market President for Gorman & Company. “The success of this important milestone will be evidenced by smiles of the first residents moving into their beautiful new homes!”You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday after the judicial custody of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday after the judicial custody of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka was extended by two more days, accusing the government of using state machinery to intimidate young protesters.In a video shared on social media, Dipke questioned the Prime Minister's leadership and praised Das and Ranka for remaining defiant despite spending five days in judicial custody."You must be feeling very strong keeping a 26-year-old Saurav Das in jail. You must be feeling very strong beating children on the streets. You must be feeling very strong putting up barricades across Delhi and dragging students on the streets," he said.Dipke claimed that Das and Ranka had gone to Jantar Mantar to wave the national flag but were sent to judicial custody. He also alleged that their court hearings had been repeatedly postponed. "Is this strength? Hiding behind the police, hiding behind the courts, is this Narendra Modi's strength?" he asked."Do you feel like a very powerful Prime Minister by keeping them in jail? You are just a coward," Dipke added.Then, praising Das for remaining composed despite his detention, Dipke said the young protester had previously admitted that he would struggle to spend even a day in jail. "After spending five days in jail, the same Saurav Das, who himself thought he would not be able to survive even a single day in jail, walks into court on the fifth day with a smile," he said."And even when he learns that his judicial custody has been extended, he is not afraid. That is strength," he added. Dipke had also shared a photo of Das smiling as he appeared in court.Read more:Dipke share photo of Das, Ranka after judicial custody extendedMeanwhile, continuing in his video statement, Dipke also praised Ranka and the families of both protesters for refusing to give in to fear. Recalling a conversation with Das's mother, he said she had told him, "I know he will be fine. He won't break so easily."He further accused the government of attempting to silence dissent through arrests and intimidation, insisting that such measures would not deter young protesters. "Mr Modi, I'm sorry to say this, none of us are scared of you. And none of us is going to remain silent," he said.Referring to his own experience of being jailed twice, Dipke added, "If you think that sending us to jail will make us stop speaking or remain silent, that is not going to happen."He also quoted a dialogue from the film Mary Kom, saying, "Don't frighten someone so much that their fear itself disappears.""You have frightened the youth of this country as much as you could. But you have frightened us so much that the fear inside us has now disappeared. So now we will not be afraid," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Reform UK's Hull and East Yorkshire elected mayor Luke Campbell is under police investigation for allegedly sharing naked images of himself.

Conservative leader of East Riding of Yorkshire Council Anne Handley said: "I think to look after the mayor, to look after himself, I think the best thing he could do was to just stand aside for now just until the investigation comes to a conclusion."

Saree said the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missiles since the escalation began now stands at more than 2,700.Elaborating on the strike targets, the Houthis claimed they used a large number of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones.The first operation reportedly targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu in two phases. articles.title: Over 45% of Saudi flights cancelled since October 8, residents scramble for alternatives
articles.summary: Residents in Saudi Arabia are being forced to rethink travel plans, take lengthy detours through neighbouring countries and adapt to remote working amid
articles.body: Residents in Saudi Arabia are being forced to rethink travel plans, take lengthy detours through neighbouring countries and adapt to remote working amid flight cancellations. According to a report by Cirium, more than 45% of flight departures from Saudi Arabian airports have been cancelled since October 8.Businesses have also been forced to adjust, while expatriates who regularly travel home on weekends are weighing their options amid uncertainty over when flights will resume.Government agencies in Riyadh have told employees to work from home starting Monday, while the 99-storey Kingdom Centre skyscraper, which houses the regional office of the International Monetary Fund, has also shifted to remote work, according to an AFP report, citing workers and two consultants.The disruption has also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel several high-profile events. Its flagship investment forum, the Future Investment Initiative (FII), was postponed until 2027 on Monday. Announcements have also been made concerning the MDLBEAST Soundstorm music festival, Riyadh Fashion Week and the Red Sea Film Festival. A star-studded tennis tournament has also been affected.Residents seek alternative routesWith Riyadh's airport closed, domestic airlines have been promoting flights from alternative airports, including Qassim, around three hours from the capital. Some residents have also travelled by road to airports in Bahrain and Qatar to enter or leave Saudi Arabia.A Riyadh resident described being diverted mid-flight during an attack on the airport."We decided to land in Jeddah," said the resident on the condition of anonymity. "From Jeddah, thank God, everything worked out, and we were able to catch a flight to Qassim."For expatriates, the uncertainty has raised concerns about how long they can manage without regular air connections. One resident, who frequently travelled to a Middle Eastern country before the closure, said: "I can cope with this situation for a month or more, but I cannot imagine it lasting much longer than that."Businesses are also finding ways to maintain operations. A Dubai-based consultant said that "no employee is forced to travel to Saudi Arabia" but if a client relationship was at risk they were "encouraged to make the trip by car via Bahrain".Western embassies have tightened travel advisories, with some warning against travelling to the kingdom. Discussions among expatriates about potentially leaving Saudi Arabia have also stirred resentment among some Saudis, who feel that wealthy foreign residents have not stood by the country during the crisis.Airport attacks deepen disruptionThe travel crisis follows a sharp escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who have targeted airports and energy infrastructure in the kingdom in recent weeks.Last week, the Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of attacking Riyadh's airport 20 times in October alone."The Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations," said coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki.A regional airline source said the carrier had been told by Saudi authorities on Friday that the airport would remain closed until further notice. A second source from another regional airline said it had been informed that the closure would last at least until October 24."When people start throwing missiles directly at Riyadh airport and any other airport, you can't just continue to operate," said Captain Desmond Ross, an aviation expert based in Dubai and Ireland with decades of experience as a pilot and air traffic controller."An attack on an airport is something entirely different from a non-aviation target," AFP reported quoting Ross."I think Riyadh has suffered that more dramatically than any other of the Gulf nations or the Arab nations," during the ongoing Middle East war.Blow to Saudi Arabia's economic ambitionsThe prolonged airport closure and the postponement of major events have also dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract international investment and diversify its economy beyond oil.For nearly a decade, the Future Investment Initiative has served as a platform for the kingdom to court global investors, business leaders and heads of state."Few want to visit a country under persistent deadly missile attacks. And even fewer want to invest in one," wrote Karen Elliott House, author of a recent book about the crown prince, in a Wall Street Journal op-ed.Saudi ministers have sought to reassure residents and investors amid growing concerns over security. Last week, as text messages warning of an attack on the capital were sent, Human Resources Minister Ahmad bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi addressed the issue at the Riyadh Economic Forum."We are safe. With God's will," he told the crowd. "May God turn their plots back against them."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Four Virginia police officers crawled through a smoke-filled house to pull an unconscious man from a burning bedroom; three needed hospital treatment, and all four have received bravery awards
articles.summary: When smoke fills a room and flames begin to spread, every second can mean the difference between life and death.
articles.body: When smoke fills a room and flames begin to spread, every second can mean the difference between life and death. In Culpeper, Virginia, four police officers faced that reality on October 3, crawling through a smoke-choked house to find a resident who had failed to escape the fire. Their search led them into a burning bedroom, where an unconscious man lay waiting to be rescued, states an online report by Fox News. The officers brought him out alive, but the rescue came at a cost, with three of them requiring hospital treatment. Scroll down to read the details of the accident.A desperate search inside the houseAccording to Fox News, the emergency unfolded that evening when officers arrived at a wooden house in Culpeper to find thick smoke pouring from its windows. Residents living in separate apartments had already made it outside, but they feared one man might still be trapped inside.Officer Ashley Sain entered the building without protective gear and began checking rooms. Officer Neal Coffey soon joined her, and the two made their way upstairs, where smoke was escaping through the gaps around a locked bedroom door.Coffey used a small tool to open the lock. As the officers called out to check whether anyone was inside, they received no response. Beyond the doorway, flames were visible through dense, black smoke. By then, Sgt. David Cole and Officer Michael Beel had also reached the second floor, adds another report by CBS Evening News.Crawling through smoke and flamesAccording to CBS Evening News, body-camera footage captured the officers' increasingly difficult search as visibility inside the bedroom deteriorated. Coffey crawled across the wooden floor with a flashlight, struggling to see through the smoke. Unable to move safely while standing, he lowered himself further and felt his way through the room.He eventually found a man lying unresponsive on a bed. The resident was breathing but could not get himself to safety, also adds the report.Coffey tried to move him towards the doorway, calling for assistance as the rescue became more difficult. Beel crawled into the room to help, while Sain and Cole joined the effort.Working together, the four officers pulled the unconscious man onto the floor and dragged him into the hallway. Firefighters soon reached them, and a team carried the resident out of the burning building before extinguishing the fire, explains Fox News report.The man was taken to a hospital and subsequently transferred to a regional burn centre. Authorities have not released his identity or the cause of the fire, citing an active investigation, adds the report.Bravery recognised after the rescueThe incident left its mark on the rescuers, too. Three of the four officers received hospital treatment for smoke inhalation and other injuries before being released later that evening.On October 14, all four officers were presented with valor awards in recognition of their actions, according to the Culpeper Police Department, adds Fox News report.The rescue highlighted the risks officers can face when responding to emergencies that fall outside their usual duties. articles.title: In 1848, a Massachusetts stone mill began making equipment for textile factories; after standing vacant, the 150,000-sq-ft landmark was restored for $53 million and converted into 86 apartments, 69 of them affordable
articles.summary: A 170-year-old stone mill that once made water turbines and machinery during New England’s industrial boom has completed a $53 million (£41 million)
articles.body: A 170-year-old stone mill that once made water turbines and machinery during New England’s industrial boom has completed a $53 million (£41 million) historic restoration. The building has reopened as an 86-unit residential complex offering homes at different price levels in Lawrence, Massachusetts. Built in 1848 by industrialist Abbott Lawrence along the Merrimack River, the 150,000-square-foot building sat empty for decades. According to case study documents published by the US National Park Service, the historic property has now been turned into Stone Mill Lofts. Of its 86 apartments, 69 are set aside as affordable housing for lower-income households. The project was funded through a mix of federal and state historic tax credits, along with Low Income Housing Tax Credits. The cost of work that qualified for rehabilitation funding came to about $44 million, within the total project budget of $53 million.Mixed-income housing and community facilitiesThe newly opened complex offers homes for people at different income levels. Of the 69 affordable apartments, 58 are reserved for low-income residents, while 11 are set aside for very low-income individuals and families. The remaining 17 apartments are rented at market rates. The renovated homes retain many of the mill’s original features, including exposed stone walls, timber ceilings and wide wooden floors. articles.title: After surviving two life-threatening brain haemorrhages, Emilia Clarke founded SameYou in 2019; seven years later, it has raised over £3.8 million and helped more than 1,200 survivors access online rehabilitation
articles.summary: For actor Emilia Clarke, surviving two life-threatening brain haemorrhages changed her understanding of recovery and the support people need after a
articles.body: For actor Emilia Clarke, surviving two life-threatening brain haemorrhages changed her understanding of recovery and the support people need after a medical crisis. In 2019, she founded the brain injury recovery charity SameYou with her mother, Jenny Clarke, to address gaps in rehabilitation and help survivors rebuild their lives. According to SameYou's 2026 Impact Report, the charity has raised more than £3.8 million since its launch and helped over 1,200 survivors access NeuroRehabilitation Online (NROL). Its work has also received recognition through the NHS Excellence Awards 2026, highlighting how online rehabilitation can extend support beyond hospital discharge.How Clarke's experience led to SameYouClarke, known for playing Daenerys Targaryen in Game of Thrones, experienced two brain haemorrhages while working on the television series. Her recovery exposed her to the physical and emotional challenges that can continue long after a patient survives a medical emergency. The experience also drew attention to the difficulties survivors face when they leave hospital without sufficient rehabilitation or long-term support. Brain injuries can affect movement, communication, memory, mental health and a person's sense of identity, making recovery a process that extends beyond immediate medical treatment.Clarke and her mother launched SameYou in 2019 to improve access to rehabilitation for people affected by brain injury and stroke. The charity works with clinicians, researchers, healthcare providers and survivors to develop practical recovery solutions. Rather than focusing exclusively on treatment immediately after an injury, SameYou aims to support people as they rebuild their lives, relationships and confidence. Its 2026 Impact Report identifies clinical rehabilitation, community support and educational resources as three central areas of its work.More than £3.8 million raised since 2019SameYou's 2026 Impact Report records total fundraising of £3,812,226 since the charity was established. The report says this investment has supported four major research projects, postgraduate training in neurorehabilitation nursing and practical programmes designed to improve access to recovery services. The charity also develops resources to help survivors understand their condition and manage challenges after leaving the hospital. These include information on sleep, nutrition, cognitive changes and social difficulties, alongside services intended to help people navigate rehabilitation and return to employment.SameYou says many survivors experience a sharp reduction in support after discharge, even though physical, psychological and social challenges can persist. Its work seeks to address this gap by combining clinical services with peer support, education and practical assistance. The charity relies on donations rather than government funding, according to its report. Its model involves working with established healthcare and research organisations to test approaches that could eventually reach more people.Online rehabilitation reaches more than 1,200 survivorsOne of SameYou's significant initiatives is NeuroRehabilitation Online, which provides group rehabilitation sessions through video calls. The programme allows NHS therapists to deliver physical, cognitive and other forms of support to participants in their own homes. The charity co-created and funded NROL with the UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology during the COVID-19 pandemic, when access to face-to-face rehabilitation was disrupted. The initiative was subsequently expanded with NHS partners in Lancashire and South Cumbria.SameYou's 2026 Impact Report states that more than 1,200 survivors have accessed NROL. The programme is intended to complement existing rehabilitation services, giving participants additional opportunities to practise skills, receive guidance and connect with others facing similar challenges. According to SameYou, the programme has expanded across NHS partner trusts and includes physical, talking and community groups led by therapy teams. Online delivery can also reduce the need for patients to travel to hospital, an important consideration for people whose mobility or energy levels remain affected by a brain injury.NHS Excellence Award recognises the programmeIn May 2026, SameYou announced that NROL had been named Regional Champion for Patient Involvement and Choice at the NHS Excellence Awards. The recognition highlighted the programme's approach to making rehabilitation more accessible and involving patients in their recovery. The award also reflects collaboration among clinicians, researchers, NHS organisations and people with lived experience. NROL was originally developed as a response to pandemic-related disruption, but it has since become an ongoing model for delivering additional rehabilitation outside traditional clinical settings.SameYou reports that the programme has supported hundreds of people affected by stroke, brain injury and other neurological conditions through its NHS partnerships. The charity's wider impact report also records 48 nurses enrolled in a postgraduate neurorehabilitation training programme.Expanding support beyond hospital dischargeSameYou's work reflects a broader challenge in healthcare: surviving a brain injury is only the beginning of recovery for many patients. Rebuilding independence can require sustained physical therapy, emotional support, social connection and help returning to work. Through NROL, peer-support initiatives and educational resources, the charity is working to make these forms of assistance more accessible. Its impact report outlines plans to extend rehabilitation provision and develop further support for survivors and their families.Seven years after its founding, SameYou has combined more than £3.8 million in fundraising with programmes intended to address gaps in recovery care. Clarke's experience helped bring attention to the issue, while the charity's partnerships have translated that awareness into practical rehabilitation initiatives for people navigating life after brain injury.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK nurse Rebecca Louise Burwood, deputy manager at Welsh care home, struck off after taking nearly £400,000 from 99-year-old resident; money allegedly spent on cosmetic surgery, car and motorhome
articles.summary: A nurse in the UK has been struck off the nursing register after a tribunal found that she abused her position of trust to take hundreds of thousands of
articles.body: A nurse in the UK has been struck off the nursing register after a tribunal found that she abused her position of trust to take hundreds of thousands of pounds from a vulnerable 99-year-old woman, with some of the money allegedly spent on personal expenses, including cosmetic surgery, a car and a motorhome.According to a report by the BBC, Rebecca Louise Burwood, who was deputy manager at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Wales, had a longstanding relationship with the woman, identified during the proceedings as Resident A. The elderly woman had no family members and relied on Burwood for companionship after suffering a fall, the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) tribunal heard.Nurse became woman's lasting power of attorneyThe tribunal heard that Burwood became Resident A’s lasting power of attorney, a legal arrangement that allows an appointed person to help make decisions on someone’s behalf. However, she continued to oversee the woman’s care without disclosing this position to her employer.The panel found that Burwood abused her position of trust and power. Evidence presented at the hearing showed that more than £370,000 was withdrawn from Resident A’s bank account over five years. The woman also transferred ownership of her house, valued at approximately £400,000, to Burwood.While some of the money was reportedly used for home improvements and bill payments, allegations were also presented that funds went towards Burwood’s personal cosmetic surgery.Money spent on a car and motorhomeAs reported by the BBC, the hearing was told that Burwood persuaded Resident A to spend more than £20,000 on a car and £9,000 on a motorhome. Burwood claimed the motorhome was purchased so that the two could go on day trips together.Defending the transactions, Burwood said Resident A had asked her to withdraw money because she wanted to make regular charitable donations of between £250 and £500 a week. Her lawyer, Victoria Rees, also argued that the woman had expressed a wish not to leave any money behind when she died.However, the woman’s bank raised concerns about the spending and froze her account. Burwood subsequently took Resident A to the branch to have the restriction lifted.Bank staff reportedly said Burwood was “almost blackmailing” the elderly woman and pressuring her to request that access to the account be restored.Safeguarding concerns led to investigationThe bank reported the incident to North Wales Police in 2023. However, no further action was taken at the time because Resident A did not want to pursue the matter.Flintshire County Council referred the case to the NMC in June 2023. Safeguarding staff later heard that Resident A was shocked by how much of her money had been spent.Other nurses also reported hearing conversations in which Burwood allegedly instructed the woman to “sign here” and said she would “give her the money back”. Burwood responded that she had asked Resident A to sign a condolence card.Resident A has since died.Tribunal finds serious misconductThe NMC tribunal concluded that Burwood had “engaged in a sustained, calculated course of conduct” and that her actions amounted to “serious misconduct”.Following the findings, Burwood was struck off the nursing register, meaning she can no longer legally practise as a nurse in the UK.Speaking to the BBC, James Bradford, operations director at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home, said the organisation supported the regulator’s decision.“We fully support the NMC's decision and, since these events, there have been changes in management, and our safeguarding policies and procedures have been reviewed to ensure the continued safety and wellbeing of everyone in our care,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Maha directs seed firms to compensate soybean farmers for verified losses
articles.summary: Maharashtra orders seed firms, including Mahabeej, to compensate soybean farmers for verified losses from poor germination within 15 days or face legal action.
articles.body: Pune: The state agriculture department has directed seed firms to compensate soybean farmers whose losses were confirmed by valid panchanamas in view of drought-related crop loss and widespread complaints of poor seed germination, warning of legal action if they did not comply within 15 days.The directive issued on Oct 16 followed multiple rounds of hearings conducted by the directorate of quality and inputs after more than 22,000 farmers, largely from Vidarbha and Marathwada, complained of poor germination of soybean seeds supplied by private firms and state-run Mahabeej. Around 1,000 complaints were lodged against Mahabeej alone.Director of quality and inputs Sunil Borkar said seed firms had questioned the authenticity of several panchanamas but were told to provide relief in cases where crop damage reports were found genuine. “Although these firms have raised objections to the accuracy of panchanamas conducted by district agriculture offices statewide, we have directed them to assist affected farmers whose panchanamas are genuine. Not all panchanamas are disputed. If the companies fail to act within a fortnight, we will consider legal action,” Sunil Borkar, director of quality and inputs, told TOI.The department has also suspended the licence of a seed firm for allegedly repackaging and selling last year’s seed stock under a new brand without mandatory testing.The compensation push comes as soybean growers grapple with severe crop losses due to deficient rainfall. Soybean cultivation crossed 50 lakh hectares this kharif season, encouraged by strong prices last year, but drought-like conditions have hit large parts of the state’s key growing regions, leaving some farmers with near-total crop failure.Farmers who experienced poor germination were forced to resow, adding to their costs. A senior agriculture official said verified claimants should receive assistance without delay. “Lakhs of growers will face massive production losses this year. Some farmers have reported zero yield, while others had to undertake resowing after poor germination. In this difficult situation, firms should help genuine claimants so that they can sustain themselves and prepare for the ongoing rabi season,” the official said.Latur farmer Sunil Bhure said he had to resow after Mahabeej seeds failed to germinate adequately. “Now is the time for the firms to help us. Poor-quality seeds forced me to resow, and the lack of rainfall later made things worse. I’ve suffered losses at every stage and can’t afford to plant any crop this rabi season. We still haven’t received any assistance from state govt,” Bhure told TOI.He said, “If Mahabeej reimburses the Rs 8,000 I spent on seeds, it will provide some relief.”Farmer groups have demanded a transparent, time-bound compensation process and greater accountability from seed firms and regulators. Experts, meanwhile, have called for scientific assessment of germination failures. “Field inspections and proper documentation should be used to determine the cause of crop failure and establish liability. This will help prevent similar issues in the future,” an expert who worked with state govt said.The experts stressed that compensation for verified seed-quality failures should be treated separately from drought relief, arguing that poor rainfall should not deny farmers compensation where seed defects have been independently established. “While deficient rainfall can reduce crop yields even when seeds are of acceptable quality, it should not prevent farmers from receiving assistance for independently established seed-quality failures,” activist Vinod Tathod from Akola said.“The effectiveness of the move will depend on how quickly verified claims are settled and whether the department follows through on its warning of legal action against companies that fail to comply,” another activist Vijay Jawandhia from Nagpur said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Shah to meet kin of 3 whose deaths revived Punjab’s drug debate
articles.summary: Amit Shah to visit Punjab, meet families of three victims linked to drug menace debate, attend Ludhiana Dussehra with ‘Ravan of Chitta’ effigy burn.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Union home minister Amit Shah will visit Punjab on Tuesday to meet the families of people whose deaths have revived the debate around the drug menace in the poll-bound state. He will also attend Dussehra celebrations in Ludhiana, where an effigy billed as the ‘Ravan of Chitta’ will be burnt. Chitta is used for heroin in local parlance.The visit has triggered a political slugfest, with AAP and Congress criticising the Centre over the smuggling of drugs from Pakistan.After landing in Amritsar, Shah will visit Mari Panwan village in Gurdaspur district at noon to meet the family of Bikramjit Singh, who was allegedly hacked to death on Oct 15 for opposing drug sales. At 1.30pm, he will travel to Toor Banjara village in Sangrur district to meet the family of Gulzar Singh, who died by suicide on Sept 7 after allegedly being harassed for questioning finance minister Harpal Cheema over drug sales in his village.Shah will then reach Mansa at 2.30pm to meet the family of anti-drug activist Parminder Singh Jhota, who was killed on Oct 13. A protest demanding justice in the case is underway in the town.The Union minister is scheduled to address the media at Punjab Agricultural University in Ludhiana at 3.30pm before attending the Dussehra function at Ramlila Ground at 4.30pm.AAP supremo Arvind Kejriwal, without naming Shah in a post on X, said the BJP could not manage law and order in its own states.Punjab finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema also targeted the BJP-led Centre over gangsterism, drug trafficking and extortion, questioning why reports of criminal activity and threatening calls linked to jailed gangster Lawrence Bishnoi continued despite his incarceration in Sabarmati Jail. “The BJP cannot evade responsibility for these issues. Cases involving murder, extortion and kidnapping have been registered against Lawrence Bishnoi in different parts of the country,” he said.Shiromani Akali Dal MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal wrote to Shah seeking a CBI probe into Jhota’s murder and a wider investigation into what she called a “politician-police-drug mafia nexus in Punjab”. She said a comprehensive probe was needed to expose drug networks and protect young people.Punjab Congress in-charge Sachin Pilot said Shah’s visit would mean little without concrete action to improve law and order. articles.title: Mann’s OSD faces 2nd round of CBI questioning; dismisses WhatsApp chats as ‘normal’ transfer requests
articles.summary: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann’s OSD Rajbir Ghuman faces 2nd CBI grilling in corruption probe, calls WhatsApp transfer chats routine; next summons Oct 22.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s officer on special duty (OSD) Rajbir Singh Ghuman faced his second round of 4.5-hour CBI questioning on Monday in connection with an ongoing corruption probe.Speaking to the media outside the agency’s office, Ghuman dismissed WhatsApp chats flagged by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) as routine requests for postings and transfers, while questioning the timeline surrounding cash-stuffed bags allegedly thrown from a Kharar high-rise apartment.It was Ghuman’s second appearance before the central agency, following a six-hour questioning last Friday. On coming out of the CBI office after the session that stretched from 2 pm to 6.30 pm, Ghuman said the CBI posed around 40 to 50 questions, some of which revisited previous inquiries. “The questioning was on similar lines to last time, and I gave satisfactory replies,” he said.Ghuman denied that WhatsApp chats recovered by the ED from businessman Nitin Gohal’s phone contained anything illicit. “Those were routine messages regarding requests for transfers and postings. They were normal messages, and there was nothing (incriminating) in them,” he said.According to the ED, Gohal’s seized phone revealed 21 WhatsApp chats relating to transfers and postings of officials between Sept 2023 and March 2026.Regarding the incident where cash-filled bags were reportedly thrown from a ninth-floor apartment belonging to Gohal at Kharar’s Western Towers Society in May, Ghuman stated that the incident had not been incorporated into the CBI investigation. He questioned how Gohal’s family could have tossed the bags an hour after being detained.“The ED itself stated in its panchnama that the bags were recovered on the road. The raid began at 7 am, and his family was taken into custody by 7.10 am. Since the bags were allegedly thrown at 8.30 am, how could they possibly have thrown them? Either someone tossed the bags out of panic, or it was a ‘drama’ by some agency.”Ghuman said he had been called again on Oct 22. “I will come again and cooperate (with CBI),” he said.Alleging an attempt to intimidate certain individuals, Ghuman said he urged CBI officials to conduct a fair probe, expressing confidence that an impartial investigation would promptly get them a clean chit.Hitting out at opposition parties, Ghuman said, “There has been no corruption—this is purely propaganda to defame us. Whenever the ED or CBI issues a letter, opposition leaders like Bikram Singh Majithia and Sukhpal Singh Khaira immediately get hold of copies and make them public.”Ghuman was earlier alleged to have skipped two summons from CBI on Oct 7 and 9. The first time, CMO said no summons was received, and in the second instance Ghuman issued a legal response to the notice but did not turn up in person.On Oct 12, SC granted Ghuman interim protection from coercive action in the case and directed him to fully cooperate with the investigation. The very next day, ED, too, registered a case in Jalandhar, adding an alleged money-laundering angle to the probe.The investigation stems specifically from a CBI case registered under directives from Punjab and Haryana high court.
